new_statements.quote: The Bantoid sub-group Mambiloid comprises some 10 different languages of which Mambila. with at least 12 different dialects and over 100,000 speakers, is the largest; among the others are Kwanja, Ndoro, Vute, and Wawa, each of which also has dialectal variation, and Tep, Mbongo Mvanip, Ndunda, Somyev, and Nizaa, none of which is reported to have demonstrable dialectal variation. While for many of these the only data available are extended wordlists, most Mambiloid languages appear to have four contrastive lexical tones; Nizaa and Vute have three lexical tones, while one distinguishing feature among Mambila lects is three as opposed to four tones.
new_statements.citation: Connell, Bruce. 2016. Lexical Tone in Proto-Mambiloid. In: 2nd International Congress 'Towards Proto-Niger-Congo: Comparison and Reconstruction' (Paris, 1-3 September 2016), Book of Abstracts (printed 28 January 2016), p. 2. Paris: LLACAN.
new_statements.locator: p. 2, 'Lexical Tone in Proto-Mambiloid', first paragraph (extract lines 8-15)
new_statements.check: not checked by the second reader
new_statements.relation_note: Hedged family-level statement: most Mambiloid languages appear to have four contrastive lexical tones; tone systems of the four-tone languages evolved independently; verbs contrast fewer tones than nouns in Nizaa/Mambila. Mvanip is named as a member without an individual tone count.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mambiloid languages, Mvanip included by name in the membership list, are lexical-tone languages; most 'appear to have four contrastive lexical tones' (Nizaa, Vute three; some Mambila lects three). Nothing on stress or accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Nizaa and Vute have three tones; some Mambila lects three rather than four; for several small languages 'the only data available are extended wordlists'
new_statements.identity_note: 'Mbongo Mvanip' = Mbongno [bgu] and Mvanip [mcj] run together (comma dropped); Connell's own 1999 Zongo Ajiya Mvanip wordlist is the datum behind it. The tone statement is family-level ('most Mambiloid languages'), not asserted of Mvanip individually. [name in source: Mbongo Mvanip (in the list 'Tep, Mbongo Mvanip, Ndunda, Somyev, and Nizaa'); pages book of abstracts p. 2 (abstract 'Lexical Tone in Proto-Mambiloid', paragraph 1)]
